scenes.sub: Understand what you're really taking on when you provide liquidity to a perpetuals exchange.

scenes.title: Key ideas
scenes.vo: Many on-chain perp exchanges let you deposit into a liquidity vault that acts as the counterparty to traders (the "house"). The vault earns trading fees, borrowing/funding fees and part of liquidations, and loses when traders win. Returns: fees + traders' losses minus traders' profits. Risks: a run of profitable traders (or a few very large ones), open interest concentrated on one side, oracle manipulation or latency, the market-making strategy of the vault (some vaults actively trade), and exchange contract risk. Check: the vault's historical P and L split (fees versus trader P and L), its open-interest caps, how it prices assets (oracle), and withdrawal rules (cooldowns, fees).

scenes.vo: A vault shows 25% A.P.R.: 18% from fees, 7% from traders' net losses over the last 6 months. In a strong one-directional trend, traders who are long win, so the vault's "trader P and L" component can swing to minus 20% or worse, wiping out the fees. Size it as an active trading exposure, not as fixed income, and check whether withdrawals are delayed in stress.

Size it as an active trading exposure, not as fixed income, and check whether withdrawals are delayed in stress.

lines: When does a perp liquidity vault lose money?
scenes.sub: Answer: When traders are net profitable, e.g. in strong trends.
scenes.vo: When does a perp liquidity vault lose money? ... Pause and think. ... The answer: When traders are net profitable, for example in strong trends.
